idiom_name: two successive dispatches (accept/visit pair) or one lookup keyed by the two types
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give the first object a dispatch method that calls a method on the second object, passing itself (accept(visitor), collideWith(other), renderOn(medium)); overload resolution or the method name encodes the receiver's concrete type, so the pair selects the code. Where both type sets are closed, replace the round-trip with a single lookup keyed by the two type tags (tag pair -> handler) or with an exhaustive match. Keep the dispatch method trivial and the pair-handler set total: a fallback for the base type, a default arm or a silently ignored lookup failure destroys the pattern's only structural guarantee. Canonicalise commutative pairs so (A,B) and (B,A) share one implementation. Prefer named methods (Style B: visitCircle, visitRectangle) over overloaded visit(Shape&) — Style B produces a compile error for missing pairs, while Style A silently falls through.
code_sketch:
collide(a, b):
    return a.dispatch(b)            # dispatch #1: receiver's runtime type

Circle.dispatch(b):
    return b.visit_circle(self)     # dispatch #2: receiver's static type + argument's runtime type

# closed type sets: handlers[canonical(type(a), type(b))](a, b)
pitfalls: Putting behaviour in the dispatch method instead of the pair handler: the handler must be the only place that knows a pair.
Adding an overload for the base type or a catch-all arm; it silently absorbs exactly the missing cells the pattern was meant to expose.
Sharing mutable state between pair handlers, which makes traversal order observable and reentrancy unsafe.
Storing a visitor by reference across scopes: the reference must remain valid for the lifetime of the dispatch — use-after-free is UB.
Missing visit overloads can evade the linker with separate compilation and weak linkage — use pure virtual (= 0) declarations, not default empty bodies.

Wrong move: hand-rolling accept/visit where the language already offers multiple dispatch (Julia methods, CLOS generic functions, C# dynamic) -> you reimplement method lookup with more code and worse caching than the runtime, and empirical studies find most hand-written candidates are false positives -> instead use the native mechanism, or verify the call site truly resolves on two runtime types before encoding the matrix.

Wrong move: giving every varying concept its own class hierarchy so the second dispatch has something to resolve -> heterogeneous collections pay a runtime lookup per pair and each new type variant multiplies specialised methods (the Julia performance guide warns against exactly this values-as-parameters proliferation) -> instead dispatch on types only where pair behaviour genuinely differs; keep the rest as tags, enums or table keys.

Wrong move: reaching for C# dynamic to get the second dispatch without a visitor interface -> missing pairs compile clean and throw RuntimeBinderException at the first production call -> instead keep the compile-time-checked visitor or a pair table whose unregistered cells fail in tests.
